system: You are an expert reviewer of machine-learning research ideas.
user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Primary question: can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone, and how much mask-supervised localisation does that retain on the unseen modality? At each of the four adapter levels, with the original level weights, the Dice and Focal terms are replaced by an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of the level's patch-to-text anomaly probabilities (k = 1% of patches), applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded; the detection adapters and their loss are unchanged. Hypothesis: because patch scores are similarities to text anchors shared by all modalities, this weak supervision yields localisation that transfers to the unseen modality. Primary outcomes: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO on the held-out folds with masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and image-level AUROC on all folds, mask-supervised versus image-label-supervised MVFA under the shared protocol. Secondary analyses: (i) a control in which the text anchors of the segmentation branch are replaced by a learned linear patch classifier trained with the same MIL loss, isolating the role of the text anchors; (ii) a per-level breakdown; (iii) two label-budget points with masks for 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images (one seed, two folds).

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Feature-space anomaly mixing: graded synthetic positives from normal-bank patches
SUMMARY: Create synthetic training patches in feature space by mixing the features of normal-bank patches with those of the gated top patches of abnormal images at random ratios, and train the segmentation adapters to output the mixing ratio, giving dense, graded patch-level supervision without image-space artefacts.
HYPOTHESIS: Adding feature-space mixing (weight 0.5) to gated MIL raises held-out AUPRO by at least 2 points over gated MIL alone, and outperforms image-space synthetic lesions (Poisson blending) under the same training budget.
RATIONALE: Gated MIL selects a few positive patches per abnormal image and leaves most of the map unsupervised. Image-space synthetic lesions add supervision but teach the model blending artefacts. An analogous trick from representation learning (mixup in feature space) avoids both: a convex combination of a normal patch feature and a likely-lesion patch feature at ratio lambda is a patch whose abnormality is known to be lambda, and such graded examples shape the adapters' output scale over the whole range, not only at 0 and 1. Because mixing happens at the input of the adapter at each level, it needs no new images and no masks.
METHOD: 1) Per batch and level: take the gated top-k patch features of abnormal images (as in gated MIL) and an equal number of random normal-bank patch features of the same dataset. 2) Mixed feature f_mix = lambda f_abn + (1 - lambda) f_nor with lambda ~ U(0, 1); pass through the level's segmentation adapter. 3) loss.py: mix_loss = BCE(p(f_mix), lambda) (soft target) added to gated MIL with weight 0.5. 4) Hyper-parameters: weight {0.25, 0.5, 1}; number of mixed patches per batch 64. Inference unchanged.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); all source masks discarded; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA and the problem's plain top-k MIL re-run under the same rule; 3 seeds, mean and std; pixel AUROC and AUPRO on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC, image AUROC on all folds. Baselines: gated MIL; gated MIL + image-space synthetic lesions. Falsified if feature mixing does not improve AUPRO over gated MIL.

Idea B:
TITLE: Learnable log-sum-exp pooling per dataset replaces fixed top-k in MIL
SUMMARY: Replace the hard top-k mean of the MIL operator by log-sum-exp pooling with a learnable temperature per source dataset, which interpolates smoothly between max and mean pooling and lets gradient descent find each dataset's effective lesion fraction from image labels.
HYPOTHESIS: Per-dataset learnable log-sum-exp pooling matches or exceeds witness-rate-adaptive top-k MIL in held-out pixel AUROC (difference >= 0) and the learned temperatures order the masked source datasets by their true lesion area fraction.
RATIONALE: Witness-rate MIL estimates the lesion fraction outside the network with a statistical estimator and then applies a hard cut. An analogous but end-to-end principle exists in weakly supervised localisation: smooth pooling operators whose sharpness is a parameter. With a learnable temperature r_d per dataset, LSE pooling (1/r) log mean exp(r p_j) behaves like max pooling for large r and like mean pooling for small r, so the image-level loss itself learns how concentrated each dataset's lesions are. Every patch receives gradient in proportion to its softmax weight, which also avoids the discontinuity of top-k.
METHOD: 1) loss.py: lse_pool(p, r) = (1/r) log(mean_j exp(r p_j)); r_d = softplus(rho_d) + 1, rho_d learnable per source dataset (init so that r = 20). 2) MIL loss: BCE(lse_pool(p_l, r_d), y) per level for every image (normal images included). 3) train_zero.py: rho_d in the seg optimizer. 4) On the held-out modality, r is not needed at test time (inference unchanged). Hyper-parameters: init r {5, 20, 50}.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out zero-shot training on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together); all source masks discarded; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA and the problem's plain top-k MIL re-run under the same rule; 3 seeds, mean and std; pixel AUROC and AUPRO on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC, image AUROC on all folds. Baselines: fixed top-k MIL; witness-rate top-k MIL. Diagnostic: learned r_d vs. true lesion area fraction. Falsified if LSE pooling is worse than witness-rate top-k.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
response:
REASONING: Idea B directly addresses the core formulation of the research problem (replacing the fixed top-k patch aggregation in the weakly supervised image-level MIL loss) using a smooth, learnable aggregation operator that directly targets varying lesion extents across BMAD's diverse datasets. In contrast, Idea A introduces generic feature mixup with an arbitrary continuous interpolation target on non-linear patch-to-text similarity adapters, introducing conceptual flaws and drifting away from solving the MIL pooling bottleneck.
CONFIDENCE: HIGH
WINNER=B
